.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 359 PM EDT Saturday...

No significant changes.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 359 PM EDT Saturday...

1. A few showers tonight but mainly dry through Tuesday.

2. Brief high pressure will give way to cyclonic flow and 
periods of showery weather through Friday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 359 PM EDT Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: An upper low remains centered just to the east heading 
into Monday, keeping the region in a seasonably cool airmass. A few 
showers will continue to move through tonight, with a bit more 
widespread coverage over Vermont as a shortwave pivots through. 
After the shortwave exits, dry conditions will prevail through 
Monday. Skies will clear and it should be a great early fall 
stretch. Radiational cooling will be efficient Sunday night, with 
lows generally falling into the 40s and upper 30s. The current 
forecast low at SLK is 37, but it could easily fall a few more 
degrees if confidence increases in light winds. Warm air advection 
will begin for Monday and Tuesday, but it will be unsuccessful in 
causing a significant airmass change, with the humidity staying low 
and temperatures remaining around seasonable. A few showers are 
possible in northern areas Monday night and early Tuesday morning as 
a dying cold front passes into the region.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A broad upper high will be positioned to our south 
during the middle of next week. Between a departing trough and 
another one moving towards James Bay, there will be a 500mb ridge 
axis that extends well north into Quebec Province. Cool air will 
remain locked in eastern Vermont Tuesday night, but clouds and warm 
advection will begin impinging across northern New York. So eastern 
Vermont will tumble into the mid 40s, along with cool hollows of the 
Adirondacks, while most the rest of the region will stay in the 50s, 
and perhaps a few spot 60s in the St. Lawrence Valley as we open up 
Wednesday. Much of Wednesday will be dry, but cloudy. Winds at 850mb 
will be speedy at 50-55 knots, but it appears we'll have a modest 
inversion below that layer. Nevertheless, the pressure gradient from 
departing surface high pressure and a sub-990mb low to our north 
will promote gusty winds (at least 25-35mph) across the region by 
Wednesday afternoon. This will likely bring some 70s into the 
region, although some raw guidance suggests temperatures may be 
towards more the upper 60s to lower 70s range. Mid to late 
afternoon, a leading surge of warm air will overrun departing cool, 
stable air and produce some rain. Synoptic guidance is likely broad-
brushing rain given the strong mid-level flow that will likely 
produce strong terrain shadowing downwind mountain areas. There's 
also plenty of dry air that must be saturated in the lower-levels. 
As we get into the range of mesoscale guidance, this will probably 
look less like a wash out. The occluded front and axis of a sharp 
upper trough will progress east late Wednesday evening into 
Wednesday night, and will be capable of additional showers and 
perhaps a thunderstorm or two.

Following this, we'll spend Thursday and Friday in cyclonic flow as 
the sub 990mb low continue east. Lingering, intermittent shower 
activity, especially in northwest facing slopes, will be possible. 
Friday's chances are somewhat more uncertain depending on how 
quickly dry air filters into Vermont and northern New York. It will 
be a notable surge of cool air behind this area of low pressure 
likely preventing day time highs from reaching the 70s for much of 
the area next Friday. Broad high pressure will establish itself 
across the weekend, signaling that the next weekend should be very 
nice.

&&

.AVIATION /19Z SATURDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
Through 18Z Sunday...Conditions are a mix of VFR and MVFR across
Vermont and northern New York with isolated to scattered showers.
This will continue through the next 5 to 8 hours with ceilings
mainly 3000-6000 ft agl. Additional rain showers will move north to
south mainly across Vermont about 02z-09z. North winds of 5 to 10
knots will trend northeast or variable at 5 knots after 22z.
Ceilings are expected to become MVFR to IFR again overnight, with
the potential for a transition from low stratus to fog at KSLK
again. The combination of daylight and departure of an upper low
will result in steadily improving conditions beyond 13z Sunday with
another day of north winds around 5 to 10 knots.

Wednesday Night: Mainly MVFR, with areas VFR possible. Chance
SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Thursday: Mainly MVFR, with local VFR possible. Chance SHRA.
